rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while limiting the late-elution penalty. The midpoint temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Lengthen only the gradient to measure how the two critical pairs respond to slope. This should spread the central cluster while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Keep the improved gradient and raise temperature by 5 °C to probe selectivity of the remaining critical pair. Higher temperature should also create more room below the 10-minute time-penalty threshold.
The critical pair converged sharply upon warming, suggesting an elution-order crossover. Test 55 °C to seek separation on the other side of that crossover while retaining the favorable run time.

After the temperature-driven order reversal, a slightly steeper gradient may open the remaining critical pair rather than compress it. Shortening to 12 minutes tests this while aiming to preserve resolution of the neighboring pair and reduce elution time.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient by one step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Watch the pair previously at R = 1.59, which may become limiting as the gradient steepens.

Trim the gradient window while restoring the slope of the fully resolved injection 5. Starting slightly higher should shorten elution times, while the final organic fraction remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Keep injection 5 as the maximum-score fallback and test a faster, hotter regime. The new limiting pair is converging with both warming and steepening, so this run tests whether an order reversal restores its separation.

The limiting pair has reversed order at 60 °C; raising the starting organic fraction may widen that separation further. This trimmed, slightly steeper gradient tests a faster method while monitoring early-peak retention and the neighboring central pair.

Probe a cooler selectivity regime using the original 10-minute gradient, with injection 5 retained as the maximum-score fallback. Cooling may separate the central cluster through a different elution order; this run will also reveal whether an earlier pair becomes limiting.

Refine injection 7 by lowering the endpoint one step, making the gradient shallower to recover its limiting pair. This should retain the improved separation of the other critical pair and may achieve full resolution faster than injection 5.

Lower the endpoint another grid step; the preceding change improved the limiting resolution from 1.12 to 1.32 while leaving the other critical pair above 1.5. This tests whether a slightly shallower gradient provides a second maximum-score method with more balanced critical-pair resolution.

Return to the low starting organic fraction and shorten the 60 °C gradient by one step to test separation beyond the observed order crossover. Monitor both adjacent central pairs; injections 5 and 12 remain maximum-score fallbacks.

Test a trimmed, shallower gradient at 40 °C, where the critical pair previously improved strongly with decreasing slope. Raising the starting fraction should offset the added retention from the shallower slope, aiming for full resolution below 10 minutes.

Lengthen injection 14 by one step to bring its slope-responsive critical pair above R = 1.5. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially establishing a fully resolved alternative at a lower temperature.

Preserve injection 5’s starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while ending the programmed ramp two minutes earlier. All peaks previously eluted before this endpoint, so this should retain full resolution without the unused high-organic portion of the gradient.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 12 to increase the limiting pair’s resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Injection 5 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test whether a higher starting fraction and intermediate temperature can rebalance the two critical central pairs in a shorter run. This is an exploratory speed optimization; monitor the early pair for compression and retain injection 5 as the fully resolved fallback.

Refine the successful 55 °C methods by pairing a higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to recover the limiting central separation. The first peaks should remain retained, and the last peak is expected below 10 minutes.

Make injection 19’s gradient shallower to lift its sole unresolved pair above 1.5, using the margin in the other critical pair. The estimated last-peak elution remains below 10 minutes, making this a candidate maximum-score method with improved resolution margins.

Test a gradient slope between the fastest fully resolved method and the steeper method that lost resolution. This probes whether elution can be shortened below 7.60 minutes while keeping both critical pairs at R ≥ 1.5.

Back off the unsuccessful steepening and preserve the slope of the fastest fully resolved method while trimming the unused gradient endpoint. The last peak previously eluted near 0.57 organic fraction, so all peaks should still elute during the gradient with CRF 1.000.

Slightly steepen injection 20’s successful gradient to reduce its last-peak time while targeting a minimum resolution around 1.6. This seeks a faster alternative with more resolution margin than injection 5, whose maximum CRF is already secured.

Lower injection 22’s endpoint one step to test a modestly shallower gradient and better separation of its first critical pair. Monitor the other critical pair, whose resolution decreases slightly with shallower slopes; the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Preserve injection 17’s fully resolved slope and temperature while trimming the unused gradient tail; its last peak should still elute during the gradient near 8.00 minutes. This targets CRF 1.000 with a larger minimum-resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method, injection 5.
